slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Responsible Data Science: Privacy, Fairness and Documentation Find the personal data Day 1: Identifiers, classification, linkage and disclosure risk Data Science Track4 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-309

slides.title: Four days take one release through every check it needs
slides.text: The course at a glance Four days take one release through every check it needs Day 1 · Find Identifiers, classification, linkage attacks, measured disclosure risk. Day 2 · Reduce Generalisation, differential privacy, budgets, synthetic data and its leakage. Day 3 · Audit Errors by group, criteria that conflict, bias types, two mitigations. Day 4 · Document Datasheet, model card, impact assessment, a rerun by a peer. Day 5 · Capstone. A release pack for a second case, a scholarship allocation model, in a public repository, reviewed for ten minutes with one disparity recomputed live.

slides.title: Every claim about risk or fairness ends in a measured number
slides.text: How this course works Every claim about risk or fairness ends in a measured number Measure, then decide Unique records, linkage success, error against budget, error rates with intervals. A control without a measurement is a hope. Reference states Every lab starts from supplied files. Nothing depends on an earlier lab, and every exercise has a safety net. Synthetic data only 60,000 invented applicants. Identifiers carry the marker SYN. No lab calls or downloads a model. AI policy. AI off for the supervised check and for Lab 1.1. In the other labs an assistant may explain a method or an error, but it does not produce the audit. In the capstone anything goes, and you defend it live.

slides.title: Yusr Housing Support Fund and its screening model, Ahliya
slides.text: One case all week Yusr Housing Support Fund and its screening model, Ahliya A fictional public fund that screens applications for housing support. Its model, Ahliya (أهلية), scores each application before an officer decides. A researcher's request Waad Al-Shehri, a university researcher, asks for row-level data on household size, income and approval. Two publications District counts for a public dashboard, and a synthetic extract for a hackathon. An audit Internal audit asks whether Ahliya misses eligible applicants more often in some groups.

slides.title: Find the personal data
slides.text: Today Find the personal data Session 1 · Personal data in an analysis Which applicant fields identify a person directly, which do it in combination, and which are sensitive Session 2 · Classification and permitted use The national classification levels, the secondary use rules, and five release controls by guarantee and cost Session 3 · Linkage attacks How a release with no names is joined to an outside file, and what a link discloses Session 4 · Measuring disclosure risk Equivalence classes, uniqueness and k, and why k alone misses what a group reveals

slides.title: Personal data in an analysis
slides.text: Session 1 Personal data in an analysis Tell direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers and sensitive attributes apart in a real table Find identifiers hiding in free-text fields Decide keep, drop or transform for each field against a stated purpose 01

slides.title: The law asks for a purpose first, then only the data that purpose needs
slides.text: Recap from DS-207 The law asks for a purpose first, then only the data that purpose needs Purpose Data collected to decide support is used for that, or for a compatible purpose under the rules. Minimisation Each field that leaves has a reason tied to the purpose. "Might be useful" is not one. Secondary use Research use has its own rules: legitimate purpose, minimum necessary, an approved request. This course goes further. DS-207 decided whether a request is lawful. Here you measure how identifying the data still is after you cut it, and you reduce that risk with numbers to show for it.

slides.title: Direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers and sensitive attributes
slides.text: Not every field identifies the same way Direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers and sensitive attributes Kind What it does In the Yusr table Direct identifier Points at one person by itself national identifier, name, mobile, e-mail, the fund's applicant number Quasi-identifier Points at one person in combination, and someone outside could know it birth date, gender, postcode, district, nationality, household size Sensitive attribute What an attacker wants to learn income, social security, disability in the household, the fund's decision Free text Can hold any of the above the officers' case notes

slides.title: Ask who outside the fund could already know the value
slides.text: How to tell a quasi-identifier Ask who outside the fund could already know the value A neighbour knows the postcode and roughly the household size An employer knows the sector and the birth date A public list may hold name, birth date, gender and postcode together If an outsider can know it, an outsider can join on it Three ordinary fields In 1990 United States census data, 87% of people were likely unique on five-digit ZIP code, gender and date of birth.

slides.title: Case notes hold identifiers that no column was meant to
slides.text: The field everyone forgets Case notes hold identifiers that no column was meant to Called back on 05-SYN-418203 about the lease. Spoke to Hind at the branch; brother handles the file. Duplicate file found under SYN5520147. 2,470 of 60,000 notes hold a mobile, a national identifier or a first name (Lab 1.1) What goes wrong. A pipeline drops the identifier columns and keeps the note "for context". The extract now carries names and numbers in free text.

slides.title: Decide each field against the question: keep, drop or transform
slides.text: Minimisation in practice Decide each field against the question: keep, drop or transform Field Decision Reason, for the question "household size, income and approval by region" birth date transform an age band answers the question postcode, district drop region is the unit of the question income transform bands of 1,000 riyals applicant number transform a study code; the key stays with the data protection officer case note drop free text holds identifiers In the reference solution 8 of 23 fields leave, kept or transformed.

slides.title: A pseudonymised extract is still personal data
slides.text: A code is not anonymity A pseudonymised extract is still personal data Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with codes; the key is kept apart Whoever holds the key can reverse it; the quasi-identifiers stay SDAIA's anonymisation guideline treats pseudonymised data as personal data and its protection as weaker than anonymisation Anonymised data must be irreversible, with the re-identification risk assessed A hash is a code too Anyone with a list of national identifiers recomputes the same hashes and finds the rows (Lab 1.1 stretch).

slides.title: Is the hashed extract still personal data?
slides.text: Checkpoint Is the hashed extract still personal data? Malak replaces each national identifier with its SHA-256 hash and removes names. Birth date, gender and postcode stay. Waad says the extract is now anonymous. What do you answer? Yes: a hash cannot be reversed, so nobody can find the person No: the hash is a pseudonym and the quasi-identifiers still single people out Yes, as long as it stays on the university's servers No, but only because names were in the original table

slides.title: Classification and permitted use
slides.text: Session 2 Classification and permitted use Assign a national classification level to an extract from its impact State when an extract may leave the fund under the secondary use rules Match five release controls to their guarantee and their cost 02

slides.title: The level follows the impact of an unauthorised disclosure
slides.text: The national classification The level follows the impact of an unauthorised disclosure Level Impact Typical content Top Secret high exceptionally serious, irreparable harm to national interests Secret medium serious harm to national interests or major losses Restricted low limited harm; the policy's examples include personally identifiable information such as names and identification numbers Public none none of the impacts above Restricted splits by scale: A a whole sector, B several entities or a group of individuals, C one entity or one individual.

slides.title: Three extracts, three levels, three answers to "may it leave?"
slides.text: On the fund's analysis server Three extracts, three levels, three answers to "may it leave?" E1 · Applicant table 60,000 rows, 23 fields, names and identifiers. Restricted B. Stays inside the fund. E2 · Research extract No names, a study code, birth date and postcode kept. Restricted B. Leaves only under conditions. E3 · Counts Approved by district and nationality: 118 cells, the smallest is 2. Restricted C until treated.

slides.title: A research extract leaves under conditions, not because names are gone
slides.text: When E2 may leave A research extract leaves under conditions, not because names are gone 1 · Request through the researcher's university, with its written approval → 2 · Purpose research or public interest, not profit → 3 · Minimum only the fields the purpose needs → 4 · Measured disclosure risk reduced, then shared under an agreement

slides.title: Five controls, each with a different guarantee and a different cost
slides.text: The controls a release can use Five controls, each with a different guarantee and a different cost Control What it guarantees What it costs Pseudonymisation nothing outside the key holder; still personal data almost nothing De-identification each record hides among at least k on the chosen fields detail, and rows suppressed Aggregation no row-level data no row-level analysis; small cells still leak Synthetic data no real row, if the generator does not copy weaker relationships; must be tested Differential privacy a bound on what any one person changes noise, and a budget that runs out

slides.title: The use decides the control, and the control decides the risk left
slides.text: Fit the control to the release The use decides the control, and the control decides the risk left Follow one applicant over years inside the fund: pseudonymisation Row-level records for an approved study: de-identification Once-a-year regional counts: aggregation A realistic file for a hackathon: synthetic data Monthly district counts on a public dashboard: differential privacy Residual risk is part of the answer The monthly dashboard spends its budget twelve times a year. The hackathon file is only as safe as the generator's leakage test.

slides.title: Which control fits the monthly dashboard?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which control fits the monthly dashboard? Bashayer wants applicants per district on a public dashboard, refreshed every month. Some districts have fewer than ten applicants a month. Which control fits best? Pseudonymise the applicant numbers before counting Suppress every count below ten each month Publish a synthetic extract instead of counts Add calibrated noise under a stated yearly privacy budget

slides.title: Linkage attacks
slides.text: Session 3 Linkage attacks Explain how a linkage attack joins a release to an outside file Run a linkage on quasi-identifiers and measure its success Name what a successful link discloses 03

slides.title: A linkage attack joins the release to a file that has names
slides.text: How a release without names is re-identified A linkage attack joins the release to a file that has names 1 · Release study code, birth date, gender, postcode, income, decision → 2 · Outside file name, birth date, gender, postcode → 3 · Join on the shared fields → 4 · Unique match a name attached to an income and a decision In the lab. A synthetic volunteers register published online: 9,000 people, 3,000 of whom applied to the fund.

slides.title: Three ordinary fields re-identify 99% of the register's applicants
slides.text: Lab 1.3, the reference run Three ordinary fields re-identify 99% of the register's applicants 3,042 register rows with exactly one match 99.2% of the 3,000 applicants correctly named 97.8% of claimed links are right The 66 wrong links harm people too. Someone who never applied is now believed to be on social security, or declined.

slides.title: What the 3,042 named records disclose
slides.text: A link is the door, not the harm What the 3,042 named records disclose Declined by the fund 1,662 On social security 420 Disability in household 267 Plus the exact monthly income of every named person.

slides.title: Coarsening one field cuts the links from 99% to 17%
slides.text: The lever that matters most Coarsening one field cuts the links from 99% to 17% Join on Claimed Correct Success Precision birth date, gender, postcode 3,042 2,976 99.2% 97.8% birth year, gender, postcode 1,595 506 16.9% 31.7% Takeaway. Not zero, and two in three claimed links are now wrong: the attacker can no longer tell which ones to trust. Day 2 finishes the job with a hierarchy and a k.

slides.title: Assume the attacker knows someone who applied
slides.text: Who the attacker is Assume the attacker knows someone who applied Prosecutor Knows a specific person is in the release and looks for their row. Journalist Has an outside file and links whoever links; does not know who applied. Insider A relative or colleague who knows exact values: birth date, household size, sector.

slides.title: Which change stops most of the links?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which change stops most of the links? Release A links 99% of the register's applicants on birth date, gender and postcode. Waad needs household size and approval by region. Which single change cuts the links most while keeping her question answerable? Replace the birth date with an age band Remove gender Replace the study code with a new random code Round income to the nearest 1,000 riyals

slides.title: Link the release to the register
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Link the release to the register Re-identify applicants by linking a release to a synthetic public register. D1_3_re_identify_applicants.ipynb Load the release and the register 3 min Join on birth date, gender and postcode 7 min Keep unique matches and score them against the truth key 7 min What the links reveal 5 min Try a coarser join 3 min ✱ Stretch: Link on the district in place of the postcode and compare the success

slides.title: Measuring disclosure risk
slides.text: Session 4 Measuring disclosure risk Compute equivalence classes, uniqueness and k for a release Compare candidate releases by record-level risk Explain why k alone misses attribute disclosure 04

slides.title: An equivalence class is everyone who looks the same on the quasi-identifiers
slides.text: Risk without an outside file An equivalence class is everyone who looks the same on the quasi-identifiers age band gender region nationality class size 31-40 F Riyadh Saudi 1,410 41-50 M Tabuk Saudi 409 51-60 F Al-Jouf Non-Saudi 1 The class size is how many people a record hides among A class of 1 is a unique record The release's k is its smallest class

slides.title: The same 60,000 people, three very different risks
slides.text: Lab 1.4, the reference run The same 60,000 people, three very different risks Release Quasi-identifiers Unique Below 5 Average risk A birth date, gender, postcode 59,458 100% 0.996 B birth year, gender, district, nationality 2,152 14.3% 0.129 C age band, gender, region, nationality 7 0.1% 0.004 All three have k = 1.

slides.title: k is a floor for the most exposed person, not an average
slides.text: What k tells you k is a floor for the most exposed person, not an average k = 5 : every record hides among at least five One unique record makes k = 1 for the whole release Report k with the share below the target and the average risk The fund's target in this course: k of at least 5 Average risk The mean of one over the class size: the chance that a prosecutor picks the right record. Release C: 0.004. Its maximum is still 1.

slides.title: A class of five that all share one value discloses it to anyone who finds the class
slides.text: When k is met and the harm happens anyway A class of five that all share one value discloses it to anyone who finds the class Homogeneity In release B, 661 of 3,241 classes of five or more have a single social security value (Lab 1.4 stretch). l-diversity Ask every class to hold at least l different values of the sensitive attribute. A partial fix: two values can still be "yes" and "almost yes".

slides.title: Write it in pandas to see the mechanism, then use a tool for the release
slides.text: Tools for disclosure risk Write it in pandas to see the mechanism, then use a tool for the release sizes = df.groupby(qi)[qi[0]].transform("size") unique = (sizes == 1).sum() k = sizes.min() below_5 = (sizes < 5).mean() avg_risk = (1 / sizes).mean() ARX A desktop and Java tool: hierarchies, k, l, t, risk models and utility. sdcMicro An R package for statistical disclosure control with risk and utility measures.

slides.title: Which release is safer?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which release is safer? Release B and release C both have k = 1. B has 2,152 unique records and C has 7. Yahya asks whether they are equally risky. What do you tell him? Yes: both have k = 1, so both expose someone B is safer because its birth year and district are more precise C is far safer, but neither meets k of five until the small classes are treated C is safe to release as it is, since seven records is negligible

slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Uniqueness and k for three releases Compute unique quasi-identifier combinations and k for three candidate releases. D1_4_compute_unique_quasi.ipynb Build the three candidate releases 5 min Equivalence class sizes 6 min Unique records, k and records below five 7 min Average re-identification risk 4 min Pick the release to treat 3 min ✱ Stretch: Measure the l-diversity of social security status in release B

slides.text: Day 1 · Three things to keep Find the personal data, then measure how identifying it still is Fields are not equal Direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers, sensitive attributes and free text each need a different decision. No names is not anonymous Three ordinary fields linked 99% of the register's applicants to their income and decision. Report risk with numbers Unique records, k, the share below five and the average risk, together.

slides.title: Release with less risk
slides.text: Today Release with less risk Session 1 · Generalisation and suppression Generalise and suppress until every record hides among five, and measure what the analysis loses Session 2 · Differential privacy for counts The promise of differential privacy, calibrated noise on counts, and the error a budget costs Session 3 · Budgets and composition Sequential and parallel composition, bounded means, and one budget spread over several queries Session 4 · Synthetic data and leakage A synthetic extract generated column by column, its utility, and the tests that show it copies people

slides.title: What did the linkage attack actually need?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 What did the linkage attack actually need? Yesterday three fields linked 99.2% of the register's applicants to their income and decision. Yahya asks what the attacker had to have. Which answer is right? The key that maps study codes back to applicants At least one direct identifier left in the release An outside file sharing birth date, gender and postcode with the release The applicants' incomes, to match them to the release

slides.title: Generalisation and suppression
slides.text: Session 1 Generalisation and suppression Generalise quasi-identifiers along a hierarchy Suppress the records that stay below k Measure the utility cost on key statistics 01

slides.title: Each quasi-identifier climbs its own hierarchy, one level at a time
slides.text: Generalisation Each quasi-identifier climbs its own hierarchy, one level at a time Level birth place 0 birth date 1989-10-20 postcode 10900 1 birth year 1989 district RYD-07 2 five-year band 1985-1989 region Riyadh 3 ten-year band 1980-1989 Every level up merges classes. The anonymisation guideline names this technique: specific values replaced by more general ones, such as ages in bands.

slides.title: Search the lattice for the least general node that meets the target
slides.text: Lab 2.1, the reference run Search the lattice for the least general node that meets the target Records below five postcode district region birth date 60,000 60,000 59,870 birth year 41,404 8,576 1,744 five-year band 13,488 1,728 293 ten-year band 7,669 738 84 Rule: suppress at most 1% of records Least general node that meets it: five-year band and region 293 records left to suppress

slides.title: Suppress the records still below five, and log how many
slides.text: The last step Suppress the records still below five, and log how many 59,707 records kept 293 suppressed (0.49%) k = 5 every record hides among five What goes wrong. The suppressed records are not random. They are the rare combinations: mostly non-Saudi applicants in small regions. The cost of the control lands on the smallest groups.

slides.title: The three key statistics moved by at most 1%
slides.text: What the analysis lost The three key statistics moved by at most 1% Statistic Before After Change Approval rate, women 0.5056 0.5054 -0.04% Approval rate, men 0.4266 0.4265 -0.02% Mean income, Northern Borders 8,211 8,128 -1.01% Mean income, Riyadh 8,313 8,313 0.00% Mean household size, non-Saudi 4.526 4.517 -0.20%

slides.title: The same register now links nobody to a single record
slides.text: The attack, rerun The same register now links nobody to a single record 99.2% → 0 register applicants linked to exactly one record, before and after treatment Identity disclosure Blocked for this outside file: every match now has at least five candidates. Attribute disclosure Not blocked: a class of five that all declined still tells the attacker the decision.

slides.title: k protects the fields you chose against the attacks you imagined
slides.text: When k-anonymity is not enough k protects the fields you chose against the attacks you imagined Homogeneity Everyone in the class shares the sensitive value. Background knowledge The attacker knows a field you did not treat as a quasi-identifier. Repeated releases Two treated versions of the same table, intersected, shrink the classes. Takeaway. Treat row-level releases as personal data under an agreement, even at k of five. For published numbers, use a control with a guarantee: Session 2.

slides.title: Suppress more, or generalise more?
slides.text: Checkpoint Suppress more, or generalise more? At five-year band and district, 1,728 records (2.9%) are below five. Waad wants to keep the district. Malak can suppress those 1,728 or move to region and suppress 293. What should she weigh? Which small groups the 1,728 are, and whether Waad's question needs the district Always the option with fewer suppressed records Always suppression, since it leaves every kept record exact Whichever option gives the higher k

slides.title: Reach k of five
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min Reach k of five Reach k of at least five and measure the change in three key statistics. D2_1_reach_k_least.ipynb Three key statistics before treatment 5 min Generalise birth date and postcode step by step 8 min Suppress what is still below five 4 min The three statistics after treatment 5 min Rerun the linkage 3 min ✱ Stretch: Find a second treatment that keeps the district, and compare its cost

slides.title: Differential privacy for counts
slides.text: Session 2 Differential privacy for counts State what the differential privacy promise covers and what it does not Add calibrated noise to counts with a library Measure the error that a budget costs 02

slides.title: The output barely depends on whether any one person is in the data
slides.text: Differential privacy The output barely depends on whether any one person is in the data Two datasets that differ by one applicant A randomised release gives almost the same distribution of outputs on both Epsilon bounds "almost": smaller epsilon, closer distributions, more privacy It holds whatever the attacker knows, including every other record What it does not promise That nothing about the population is learnt. A count shows that a district has many approvals; that is the point of publishing it.

slides.title: Noise is scaled to the most one person can change the answer
slides.text: How much noise Noise is scaled to the most one person can change the answer 1 · Sensitivity adding one applicant changes one district count by 1 → 2 · Scale sensitivity divided by epsilon → 3 · Noise drawn from a Laplace distribution with that scale epsilon 1 scale 1: typical error about one applicant epsilon 0.5 scale 2 epsilon 0.1 scale 10: typical error about ten

slides.title: The library builds the measurement and tells you what it spends
slides.text: Lab 2.2 in five lines The library builds the measurement and tells you what it spends import opendp.prelude as dp dp.enable_features("contrib") domain = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int), size=59) meas = dp.m.make_laplace(domain, dp.l1_distance(T=int), scale=1 / eps) released = meas(counts) # 59 noisy counts meas.map(d_in=1) # the epsilon spent when one person changes Check the claim with the library. map computes the privacy loss from the domain, the distance and the scale. Never trust an epsilon typed in a report.

slides.title: Ten times less budget costs about ten times more error
slides.text: Lab 2.2, the reference run Ten times less budget costs about ten times more error epsilon Mean absolute error 95th percentile Relative error, ten smallest districts 0.1 9.98 30 16.0% 0.5 1.92 6 3.1% 1.0 0.85 3 1.5% 59 districts, 27,189 approved applicants, smallest district 36. 300 repeated releases per budget.

slides.title: Choose the smallest budget that meets the accuracy the use needs
slides.text: From a curve to a decision Choose the smallest budget that meets the accuracy the use needs The use: a dashboard that compares districts The rule agreed with Bashayer: typical error under 5% in the smallest districts 0.1 fails (16%), 0.5 meets it (3.1%), 1.0 meets it with margin Recommendation: epsilon 0.5 per release The budget is per release A monthly refresh at 0.5 spends 6 a year. Session 3 is about that.

slides.title: Anything computed from a released value spends no more budget
slides.text: After the noise Anything computed from a released value spends no more budget Clamp Negative counts set to zero. Round Whole numbers for a dashboard. Aggregate Regional totals summed from district counts. What goes wrong. Recomputing from the true data "to fix" a strange noisy value is not post-processing. It spends budget, usually without anyone noticing.

slides.title: What does a smaller epsilon buy?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does a smaller epsilon buy? Malak releases the 59 district counts at epsilon 0.1 instead of 0.5. Bashayer asks what changed. Which statement is right? The large districts now carry most of the error The counts are now private, where before they were not The noise is 59 times larger, one share per district Each count's noise is about five times larger, and the guarantee is stronger

slides.title: District counts at three budgets
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · 25 min District counts at three budgets Release district counts at three budgets and plot the error. D2_2_release_district_counts.ipynb True counts of approved applicants by district 4 min One noisy release with the library 6 min Repeat at three budgets 7 min Plot the error against the budget 5 min Recommend a budget 3 min ✱ Stretch: Post-process the counts (no negatives, whole numbers) and check that the error does not grow

slides.title: Budgets and composition
slides.text: Session 3 Budgets and composition Add up privacy loss under sequential and parallel composition Release a bounded mean with a library Allocate one budget across queries by need 03

slides.title: Epsilons add up over the same people, not over different people
slides.text: Spending a budget Epsilons add up over the same people, not over different people Sequential composition Two releases about the same applicants: the epsilons add. Mean income at 0.3 and household size at 0.2 spend 0.5. Parallel composition Releases about disjoint people: the largest epsilon counts once. 13 region counts at 0.1 spend 0.1, not 1.3.

slides.title: Four queries share it, and each has its own sensitivity
slides.text: Yahya's approved budget: epsilon 1 for the year Four queries share it, and each has its own sensitivity Query Released One applicant changes it by Q1 applicants per region, 13 counts 1 in one count Q2 mean income, clamped to 0 to 30,000 riyals sum by 30,000; count by 1 Q3 approved per district, 59 counts 1 in one count Q4 mean household size, clamped to 1 to 12 sum by 12; count by 1 A mean is a noisy sum over a noisy count, each with half the query's epsilon.

slides.title: An equal split wastes budget on the queries that do not need it
slides.text: Lab 2.3, the reference run An equal split wastes budget on the queries that do not need it Q3 district counts 2.05% Q1 region counts 0.24% Q2 mean income 0.05% Q4 mean household 0.04% Mean relative error with epsilon 0.25 each.

slides.title: Give each query budget in proportion to its error at epsilon 1
slides.text: Allocate by need Give each query budget in proportion to its error at epsilon 1 Query Equal: epsilon Equal: error By need: epsilon By need: error Q1 0.25 0.24% 0.099 0.61% Q2 0.25 0.05% 0.025 0.57% Q3 0.25 2.05% 0.857 0.54% Q4 0.25 0.04% 0.019 0.53% Takeaway. The worst error falls from 2.05% to 0.61% for the same total budget.

slides.title: Let the library keep the ledger, and check it adds up to the budget
slides.text: Accounting Let the library keep the ledger, and check it adds up to the budget {'Q1': 0.099426, 'Q2': 0.024857, 'Q3': 0.856597, 'Q4': 0.01912} total 1.0 Each value is map of the measurement, not a typed number Q2 and Q4 each sum two measurements: the sum and the count The ledger goes into the release log, with the date and the approver

slides.title: Monthly releases from one yearly budget make every release noisier
slides.text: The cost of repetition Monthly releases from one yearly budget make every release noisier 0.61% → 7.2% worst mean relative error, one yearly release against twelve monthly releases from the same budget The decision is Bashayer's Fresher numbers or more accurate numbers. The budget makes the trade visible instead of hiding it in suppression rules.

slides.title: How much did the region counts spend?
slides.text: Checkpoint How much did the region counts spend? Malak releases applicants per region, 13 counts, each with noise of scale 10 (epsilon 0.1 for a count). Every applicant is in exactly one region. What has the release spent? 1.3, the sum over the 13 regions 0.1, because the regions hold disjoint applicants About 0.008, a thirteenth of 0.1 Nothing, since counts are aggregates

slides.title: Split one budget over four queries
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · 25 min Split one budget over four queries Split one budget across four queries and justify the allocation. slides.title: Synthetic data and leakage
slides.text: Session 4 Synthetic data and leakage Generate a synthetic extract by sequential modelling Measure its utility against the real table Test it for record copying and membership inference 04

slides.title: A synthetic extract keeps the patterns and replaces the people
slides.text: A different kind of release A synthetic extract keeps the patterns and replaces the people Fit a model of the table, then sample new rows from it Useful where the analyst needs rows: a hackathon, teaching, testing a pipeline No row is a real person, if the model did not memorise them That "if" is tested, every time, before release No guarantee by default An ordinary generator gives no formal privacy guarantee. A generator trained with differential privacy does, at a cost in utility.

slides.title: Each column is drawn from a tree fitted on the columns before it
slides.text: How the lab's generator works Each column is drawn from a tree fitted on the columns before it 1 · age drawn from observed ages → 2 · gender tree on age → 3 · ... tree on all earlier columns → 4 · decision value taken from a training row in the same leaf What goes wrong. If a leaf may hold a single training row, the "donor" is always that row: the synthetic row becomes a copy of a real person.

slides.title: Measure utility on the shares and on a model trained on synthetic rows
slides.text: Is the file useful? Measure utility on the shares and on a model trained on synthetic rows Marginal distance Total variation distance between real and synthetic shares of each categorical column, averaged. 0 is identical. Train synthetic, test real A model predicting the officer's decision, trained on synthetic rows and scored on real rows it never saw. Compare with the same model trained on real rows: AUC 0.936.

slides.title: Compare distances to the training rows with distances to unseen rows
slides.text: Does the file leak? Compare distances to the training rows with distances to unseen rows Exact copies Synthetic rows identical to a training row, against the same share for holdout rows. Distance to closest record Share of synthetic rows closer to the training set than to the holdout. 50% means no preference. Membership inference Score each real record by its nearest synthetic row. AUC 0.5 means the attacker cannot tell members.

slides.title: The most useful file is the one that copies people
slides.text: Lab 2.4, the reference run The most useful file is the one that copies people Setting Marginal distance AUC, synthetic-trained Copies of training rows Copies of holdout rows Membership AUC leaf = 1 0.006 0.935 92.8% 0.08% 0.819 leaf = 200 0.006 0.933 0.10% 0.05% 0.511 Utility alone would pick the wrong file. Both look equally useful; one of them is 93% real people.

slides.title: Release the leaf = 200 file for the hackathon, under stated limits
slides.text: The recommendation Release the leaf = 200 file for the hackathon, under stated limits Passes : copies near baseline, membership AUC 0.511, utility within 0.003 AUC Limits : for prototypes, not for statistics about small groups Not a guarantee : one attack was tested; the report says so Rejected : leaf = 1, which copies 92.8% of rows LO4 evidence The utility and leakage report that Lab 2.4 saves, with this recommendation and its limits.

slides.title: Which result should block the release?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which result should block the release? A vendor's synthetic file matches the real one on utility. No row is an exact copy, and 31% of its rows are closer to the training data than to a holdout. What do you conclude? Nothing blocks it on these tests: no copies, and no preference for training rows It leaks: 31% of rows sit next to training records It is too accurate to be private, so it must be copying It is differentially private, since no row is copied

Differential privacy A guarantee whatever the attacker knows; error near one over epsilon; a budget that adds up. Synthetic data Rows without people only if tested: copies, distance and membership against a holdout.

slides.title: For a support decision, the two errors do different harm
slides.text: What an audit counts For a support decision, the two errors do different harm False negative An eligible applicant declined by Ahliya. The harm the fund exists to prevent. FNR = missed eligible / all eligible. False positive Support passed to someone not eligible. A cost to the fund, caught later by an officer. FPR = wrongly passed / all not eligible. In the reference data: 12,000 reviewed applications, 6,341 eligible, 5,280 passed by Ahliya at a threshold of 0.5.

slides.title: Every rate gets an interval, and small groups get wide ones
slides.text: Recap from DS-204 and DS-207 Every rate gets an interval, and small groups get wide ones A rate from 2,413 eligible women is precise A rate from 4 eligible applicants is a guess The Wilson interval stays inside 0 to 1 and behaves for small counts Report the count beside every rate Same 50% rate From 200 eligible: 43% to 57%. From 4 eligible: 15% to 85%.

slides.text: How far to slice Each extra attribute splits the data until the rates mean nothing 23 of 52 region by gender by nationality cells with fewer than 30 eligible applicants Al-Jouf, non-Saudi women 4 eligible, 3 missed: FNR 75%, interval 30% to 95%. Report "too few to estimate (4)", not 75%. What goes wrong. Fifty-two cells, one of them extreme by chance, and a headline about Al-Jouf. Many comparisons produce false alarms; small cells produce loud ones.

slides.title: One sentence: the group, the rate, the interval, the comparison, the limit
slides.text: Reporting a finding One sentence: the group, the rate, the interval, the comparison, the limit Ahliya declines 30% of eligible non-Saudi women (95% interval 25% to 35%) against 22% of all other eligible applicants; gender alone shows no gap, so the margins understate it. Rate and interval Never a bare percentage. Against whom The comparison group is named. What is not claimed No cause yet: that is Session 3.

slides.title: Four criteria, each reasonable, each equalising something different
slides.text: What "fair" can mean Four criteria, each reasonable, each equalising something different Criterion Equal across groups Plain words Demographic parity selection rate pass the same share of each group Equal opportunity false negative rate miss eligible people equally often Equalised odds false negative and false positive rates both errors equal Predictive parity precision a pass is equally reliable for each group

slides.title: Eligibility is more common among women applicants than among men
slides.text: The fact that forces a choice Eligibility is more common among women applicants than among men Women 59.7% Men 49.3% Share eligible after full review (Lab 3.2) Women applicants are more often heads of lower-income households in this data When base rates differ, a model that is not perfect cannot satisfy all criteria at once

slides.title: At one threshold, misses are equal and selection is not
slides.text: Lab 3.2, the reference run At one threshold, misses are equal and selection is not Threshold 0.5 for all Selection FNR Precision Women 50.1% 22.7% 92.3% Men 40.9% 22.8% 93.0% Gap +9.1 pts -0.2 pts -0.8 pts Equal opportunity holds almost exactly; demographic parity does not.

slides.title: Equal selection makes Ahliya miss eligible women far more often
slides.text: Force demographic parity Equal selection makes Ahliya miss eligible women far more often Equal selection (thresholds 0.620 and 0.432) Selection FNR Precision Women 44.0% 30.9% 93.8% Men 44.0% 18.5% 91.4% Gap 0 +12.4 pts +2.4 pts The trade. One gap closes, another opens. Here the gap that opens is in the harmful error.

slides.title: Choose the criterion from the decision and the harm of each error
slides.text: How to choose Choose the criterion from the decision and the harm of each error SDAIA's AI Ethics Principles ask that fairness metrics be chosen at design time from the kind of decision and the harm and benefit of correct and incorrect predictions Ahliya allocates support by need; the harmful error is the missed eligible applicant So: equal opportunity, with the selection gap explained by need When parity fits When need is believed equal and the labels are suspect, or when a fixed opportunity is shared out.

slides.title: Which criterion for a support decision?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which criterion for a support decision? Ahliya decides who is passed to an officer for housing support. Eligible applicants are more common among women. Bashayer asks which fairness criterion the fund should commit to. Equal false negative rates: miss eligible applicants equally in each group Equal selection rates: pass the same share of women and men All three criteria at once, to be safe None: Ahliya does not use gender, so it is fair

slides.text: Session 3 Bias across the lifecycle Place a finding in a stage of the AI system lifecycle Name its bias type from the national bias guide Run the check that separates two neighbouring types 03

slides.title: The AI Ethics Principles name four stages, and bias can enter at each
slides.text: Where bias enters The AI Ethics Principles name four stages, and bias can enter at each 1 · Plan and Design purpose, target, the fairness metric and its threshold → 2 · Prepare Input Data collection, recording, labels → 3 · Build and Validate features, model choice, evaluation → 4 · Deploy and Monitor use, feedback, retraining

slides.title: SDAIA's AI Bias Reference Guide defines more than a hundred bias types
slides.text: The national vocabulary SDAIA's AI Bias Reference Guide defines more than a hundred bias types Type In the guide's terms Historical Bias training data carries past circumstances that no longer hold Measurement Bias values systematically over- or under-recorded Labeling Bias labels shaped by the people who assigned them Evaluation Bias evaluation data or metrics that do not reflect real use Feedback Loop Bias the system's outputs become its future inputs

slides.title: The same gap can have two causes that need opposite fixes
slides.text: Why the type matters The same gap can have two causes that need opposite fixes Measurement or labelling? Measurement: a feature is recorded wrongly (fix the recording). Labelling: the outcome used for training is wrong (fix the labels). Historical or labelling? Historical: labels followed a rule that has since changed (retrain on the current rule). Labelling: labels were wrong when made (relabel or review).

slides.text: Lab 3.3, the reference run Two findings sit outside the data: in validation and in deployment Evaluation Bias · Build and Validate The validation report claimed accuracy 0.881 on officers' decisions in Riyadh and Makkah. Against the reviewed outcome: 0.845 there, 0.850 elsewhere. Feedback Loop Bias · Deploy and Monitor 37.4% of applications are auto-declined and never reviewed, so they never get a label. slides.text: Checkpoint Measurement or labelling? Self-employed applicants are missed by Ahliya far more often. Labeling Bias: retrain on corrected decisions Sampling Bias: reweight the self-employed in training Historical Bias: retrain on recent applications only Measurement Bias: record net income for the self-employed

slides.title: Mitigation and its cost
slides.text: Session 4 Mitigation and its cost Apply reweighting before training Apply group thresholds after training Compare accuracy and disparity, and recommend 04

slides.title: You can act before training, during it, or after it
slides.text: Mitigation You can act before training, during it, or after it Before: pre-processing Change the training data: reweighting, resampling, relabelling, fixing a feature. During: in-processing A constraint in the fitting, such as Fairlearn's reductions. Named here, not practised. After: post-processing Change the decision rule: a threshold per group.

slides.title: Reweighting makes group and label independent in the training data
slides.text: Pre-processing Reweighting makes group and label independent in the training data pg = df["group"].value_counts(normalize=True) py = df["y"].value_counts(normalize=True) pgy = df.groupby(["group", "y"]).size() / len(df) idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([df["group"], df["y"]]) w = (pg[df["group"]].to_numpy() * py[df["y"]].to_numpy() / pgy.reindex(idx).to_numpy()) model.fit(X, y, logisticregression__sample_weight=w) Rare combinations, such as approved non-Saudi women, weigh more The weights average 1 It can only fix what the labels' balance causes

slides.title: A threshold per group, tuned on one half and reported on the other
slides.text: Post-processing A threshold per group, tuned on one half and reported on the other Target: each group's FNR equal to the overall 22.5% Tuned thresholds: non-Saudi women 0.468, Saudi women 0.511, non-Saudi men 0.470, Saudi men 0.499 Reported on reviewed applications not used to tune A legal question, not only a technical one The rule now uses gender and nationality at the moment of decision. The data protection officer and legal counsel decide whether that is allowed and how it is explained.

slides.title: Thresholds narrow the gap a little; reweighting barely moves it
slides.text: Lab 3.4, the reference run Thresholds narrow the gap a little; reweighting barely moves it Reported on 6,050 reviewed applications Accuracy Largest FNR gap FNR, non-Saudi women Baseline 84.5% 12.9 pts 34.9% Reweighting 84.5% 12.6 pts 34.9% Group thresholds 84.5% 10.0 pts 32.2% Accuracy did not fall. The cost here is not accuracy: it is a rule that uses protected attributes, and a gap that remains.

slides.title: Fix the source, use thresholds only as an interim, and say what remains
slides.text: The audit's recommendation Fix the source, use thresholds only as an interim, and say what remains 1 · Source verify or impute income properly; net income for the self-employed → 2 · Interim group thresholds, if legally approved, with officer review of declines → 3 · Monitor review a sample of auto-declines, so retraining sees its misses

slides.title: Which mitigation would you recommend?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which mitigation would you recommend? Reweighting moved the FNR gap from 12.9 to 12.6 points. Group thresholds moved it to 10.0, at the same accuracy. The gap comes mostly from missing and mis-recorded income. What do you recommend to Bashayer? Group thresholds as the permanent fix, since accuracy did not fall Fix income recording first; thresholds only as an approved interim measure Reweighting, because pre-processing is always preferable Neither, since the gap is not closed completely

slides.text: Session 1 Datasheets List what a datasheet of a de-identified release must answer Fill each answer from a log, not from memory Test a datasheet for completeness 01

slides.title: A file without its documentation invites the wrong use
slides.text: What a recipient cannot see A file without its documentation invites the wrong use Waad receives 59,707 rows: she cannot see the 293 suppressed records She cannot see that income is as recorded, overstated for the self-employed She cannot see that the officer decision is historical, not a reviewed outcome The datasheet answers Why the data exist, what is in them, how they were made and treated, what risk remains, and what they must not be used for.

slides.title: Seven sections, two of them for de-identified data
slides.text: The sections Seven sections, two of them for de-identified data Motivation Who asked, for what purpose, who approved. Composition Records, fields released and removed. Collection The source and what its fields really record. De-identification Risk before, treatment, risk after, utility. Residual risk What the treatment does not cover. Uses · Maintenance Two sections: allowed and forbidden uses; contact and code.

slides.title: Fill the datasheet from the release log, never from memory
slides.text: Where the numbers come from Fill the datasheet from the release log, never from memory Release log entry Value Unique on birth date, gender and postcode, before 59,458 Linkage success, before 99.2% Suppressed (rule: at most 1%) 293 k after treatment · links claimed 5 · 0 Largest change: mean income, Northern Borders -1.01%

slides.title: "k = 5" means little without what it was measured on
slides.text: One number is not a guarantee "k = 5" means little without what it was measured on The quasi-identifiers: birth band, gender, nationality, region The suppression: 293 records, and who they were What k does not cover: a class that shares one income or one disability value Residual risks in the log Attribute disclosure in classes with one value; outside files holding other fields; suppression falling on non-Saudi applicants in small regions. What goes wrong. A datasheet that says "anonymised" and stops there. The extract is still personal data and stays Restricted.

slides.title: Name what a reader still cannot rerun, and why
slides.text: The honest last section Name what a reader still cannot rerun, and why The treatment The source stays inside the fund. Acceptable: the code and seed 309 are named. The linkage test Needs the register and the truth key, which the fund keeps for audit. The study codes Only the data protection officer holds the mapping, by design.

slides.title: What must the residual risk section say?
slides.text: Checkpoint What must the residual risk section say? Malak's draft says: "k = 5 was reached, so the extract is anonymous and no risk remains." Yahya sends it back. That k should be raised to 10 before release That the sharing agreement makes residual risk irrelevant That 99.2% of applicants can still be linked The risks k does not cover, and that the extract is still personal data

slides.title: Impact assessment
slides.text: Session 3 Impact assessment Score a risk's likelihood and impact on the national framework's scales Choose a treatment and score the residual risk Name a human reviewer for every high risk 03

slides.title: Identify, assess, treat, monitor: and assess again after treatment
slides.text: National AI Risk Management Framework Identify, assess, treat, monitor: and assess again after treatment 1 · Identify the risk, who is affected, the evidence → 2 · Assess likelihood × impact, a level and a band → 3 · Treat avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept → 4 · Monitor the residual risk, its owner, its reviewer

slides.title: Two scores from 1 to 4, and their product is the level
slides.text: The scales Two scores from 1 to 4, and their product is the level Score Likelihood Impact 1 Rare Low: limited, contained quickly 2 Unlikely Medium: tangible, contained in reasonable time 3 Likely High: substantial, needs an organisational response 4 Almost certain Catastrophic: severe, wide, possibly irreversible Bands: 1 to 2 low · 3 to 6 medium · 8 to 12 high · 16 catastrophic.

slides.title: Argue every score from a measured number
slides.text: A score needs a reason Argue every score from a measured number R2 · wrongful declines Likelihood 4: it is happening now, 30% of eligible non-Saudi women declined. Impact 3: support delayed or lost. Level 12, high. R4 · the synthetic file Likelihood 2: only a regeneration with another setting copies rows. Impact 3: leaf one copied 92.8%. Level 6, medium. What goes wrong. Scores by feeling, then adjusted until the table looks balanced. The register check in Lab 4.3 rejects a reason with no number in it.

slides.title: A useful gap says where, by how much, and what to write
slides.text: Recording a gap A useful gap says where, by how much, and what to write Where load(), the notna() filter. Effect Gap -2.9 with the filter, +0.6 without it. Fix Keep the rows, or state the filter and who it removes. What goes wrong. "Results not reproducible." True, and of no use to the author.

slides.title: On all rows at 0.5, no gender gap: the claim does not hold
slides.text: The corrected result On all rows at 0.5, no gender gap: the claim does not hold On all 12,000 reviewed applications at Ahliya's threshold of 0.5, the false negative rate is 0.227 for women and 0.228 for men (gap -0.002, 95% bootstrap interval -0.020 to +0.018, seed 309).

slides.title: Which gap explains the different number?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which gap explains the different number? A peer reports an FNR gap of -2.9 points; your rerun on all rows at 0.5 gives -0.2. The bootstrap is unseeded, the threshold is 0.45, and 633 rows with missing income are dropped. The dropped rows: removing them alone takes the gap from +0.6 to -2.9 The unseeded bootstrap, because each run differs The threshold of 0.45, because it differs from the documented 0.5 A different pandas version on the peer's machine
